questions.prompt: With the tiny tokenizer, "I am unhappy" is 4 tokens but "I am unhapy" is 7. Why does the typo cost more?
options: The tokenizer counts the typo twice to warn about it
No longer piece matches "hapy", so it falls back to one token per letter
Typos are stored as special error tokens worth 3 each
The space before "un" is dropped, adding three tokens
questions.explanation: Neither "happi" nor "happy" matches "hapy", so the tokenizer uses the single-letter tokens h, a, p and y. That turns 1 token into 4, giving 7 instead of 4.

questions.prompt: Using the rule of thumb of about 4 characters per token, roughly how many tokens is a 6,000-character English document?
questions.explanation: 6,000 characters divided by 4 characters per token is about 1,500 tokens. It is only an estimate; code and other languages usually take more tokens.

questions.prompt: Why do providers measure prices and limits in tokens rather than in words?
options: Because the model reads and writes token numbers, so tokens are what it actually processes
Because tokens are always exactly one word long
Because words cannot be stored in a computer
Because tokens are cheaper to send over the network than letters
questions.explanation: A model never sees letters or words, only lists of token numbers. The work it does, and so the cost and the limits, grows with the number of tokens.
